sample_rows.text: One thing to keep in mind when examining these qq plots is that the tails will tend to deviate from the line even if the underlying distribution is truly normal and no matter how big the N is.  This is implied in [Maarten's answer][1].  This is because as N gets larger and larger the tails will be farther and farther out and rarer and rarer events.  There will therefore always be very little data in the tails and they will always be much more variable.  If the bulk of your line is where expected and the tails deviation then you can generally ignore it.\\n\\nOne way I use to help students learn how to assess their qq plots for normality is generate random samples from a distribution known to be normal and examine those samples.  There are exercises where they generate samples of various sizes to see what happens as N changes and also ones where they take a real sample distribution and compare it to random samples of the same size.  The [TeachingDemos][2] package of R has a test for normality that uses a similar kind of technique.\\n\\n    # R example - change the 1000 to whatever N you would like to examine\\n    # run several times\\n    y <- rnorm(1000); qqnorm(y); qqline(y)\\n\\n\\n  [1]: http://stats.stackexchange.com/a/63324/601\\n  [2]: http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/TeachingDemos/index.html

I am building a natural language understanding component for a dialog system. The input is a natural language sentence (usually a short one), and the output should be a set of zero or more classes from a pre-specified set. For example: \\n\\n    input: "I offer a salary of 20000 per month for work as a programmer with a company car"\\n    output: ["OFFER(Salary=20000)", "OFFER(Job=programmer)", "OFFER(Car=yes)"]\\n\\nI collected some examples from real dialogs, in order to train a classifier. My current approach is:\\n\\n - Features: I take the words of each sentence as features (I also tried word bi-grams and letter n-grams but the performance was worse).\\n - Training: I train a separate binary classifier for each class. As positive examples, I take all sentences that have this class, and as negative examples, I take all sentences that don't have this class.\\n - Running: I run each of the binary classifiers on the new sample, and return the set of classes that correspond to the classifiers that answered 'yes'.\\n\\nThis approach lead to too many false positives. Since my dataset contains many sentences with many classes (about 6 classes per sentence), the classifier gets confused between words that belong to different classes. For example, it takes the words "work as a programmer" as positive signal to the class "OFFER(Salary=20000)", because they appeared together in many training samples.\\n\\nSo, I edited my training data and separated each sample sentence to several sub-sentences, such that each sub-sentence matches just one class:\\n\\n    input: "I offer a salary of 20000 per month"\\n    output: ["OFFER(Salary=20000)"]\\n    input: "for work as a programmer"\\n    output: ["OFFER(Job=programmer)"]\\n    input: "with a company car"\\n    output: ["OFFER(Car=yes)"]\\n\\nThe new approach lead to too many false negatives: since every sentence is a negative example of all classes except its own class, the classifier takes the words "a salary of 20000" as negative signal to the class "OFFER(Job=programmer)". Therefore, for compound sentences such as  "I offer a salary of 20000 per month for work as a programmer with a company car", the classifier finds a single class and misses all other classes.\\n\\nAny suggestions for solution will be welcome...\\n\\nNOTE: I use the winnow classification algorithm, which currently has the best score (I also tried Naive Bayes, SVM, neural network and perceptron).\\n\\n--\\n\\nSome numbers:\\n\\n - Performance of classifier trained on multi-class sentences and tested on  single-class sentences: Precision=69% Recall=97% F1=81%\\n - Performance of classifier trained on single-class sentences and tested on  multi-class sentences: Precision=99% Recall=32% F1=48%\\n\\n

There are a few errors here. Basically you put the $\\sigma^2$ in the wrong place.

Note that technically speaking you should really have $f(x|yz)$ and not $f(x|y)$ in the integral formula. Although we will see that for your specific representation the result as you have written it is still true using $f(x|y)$.

The distribution $p(\\beta|\\sigma^2,\\tau_1^2,\\dots,\\tau_p^2)$ and $p(\\sigma^2,\\tau_1^2,\\dots,\\tau_p^2)$ are both inconsistent with the integral formula you provide. The first mistake is that the latent variable distribution should also be conditional on $\\sigma^2$, so you should have $p(\\tau_1^2,\\dots,\\tau_p^2|\\sigma^2)$. In relating this to the general integral forumla you have $z=\\sigma^2,y=\\tau_j^2,x=\\beta_j$ for $j=1,...,p$.

In your definition of $p(\\beta|\\sigma^2)$, the value of $a$ should be $a=\\frac{\\lambda}{\\sqrt{\\sigma^2}}=\\frac{\\lambda}{\\sigma}$ in order for you to use the integral result. Now note that $a$ does not appear in the term $\\frac{z^2}{2s}$ inside your integral result. This is the normal distribution part so you can remove $\\sigma^2$ from the distribution $p(\\beta|\\sigma^2,\\tau_1^2,\\dots,\\tau_p^2)$. So you have:

$$ \\begin{align*} \\boldsymbol{\\beta} | \\sigma^2, \\tau_1^2, \\dots, \\tau_p^2 &\\sim N_p(\\mathbf{0}_p, \\mathbf{D}_{\\boldsymbol{\\tau}}), \\\\ \\mathbf{D}_{\\boldsymbol{\\tau}} &= \\text{diag}(\\tau_1^2, \\dots, \\tau_p^2) \\end{align*} $$

This confirms the previous note that $f(x|z)=\\int_{Y}f(x|y)f(y|z)$ holds for your specific representation. For a different representation where this isn't true, make the change of variables $s=ra$ in the integral. The other term is straigh-forward, and an exponential density with rate parameter $\\frac{a^2}{2}=\\frac{\\lambda^2}{2\\sigma^2}$. So the product should be:

$$f(\\tau_1^2,\\dots,\\tau_p^2|\\sigma^2)=\\prod\\limits_{j=1}^{p}\\frac{\\lambda^2}{2\\sigma^2}\\exp\\left(-\\frac{\\lambda^2}{2\\sigma^2}\\tau_j^2\\right)$$

UPDATE

On having a bit more think about it, the end result you have is actually correct, because if $\\tau_j^2\\sim Expo\\left(\\frac{\\lambda^2}{2\\sigma^2}\\right)$ then we also have that $\\sigma^2\\tau_j^2\\sim Expo\\left(\\frac{\\lambda^2}{2}\\right)$. This shows that the result is correct. You can also make a change of variables in your integral definition of $s=r\\sigma^2$ and you have:

$$\\frac{a}{2}e^{-a|z|} = \\int_0^\\infty \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi r\\sigma^2}}e^{-z^2/(2r\\sigma^2)}\\frac{a^2\\sigma^2}{2}e^{-a^2r\\sigma^2/2} dr, \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ a>0$$

This is consistent with your answer, by setting $r=\\tau_j^2$
